steps.say: No time given, so reach for \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\).

steps.hint: Mass times the size of the deceleration.

steps.done: Kinematic equation then F = ma: the Gold move.

gold.display: A 1000 kg car brakes from 20 m/s to rest in 40 m. Find the braking force. Use v² = u² + 2as.

steps.done: Back to 3.0 m/s², so F = 750 N. That is the whole Bronze move.
steps.hint: Divide your force by the mass.

bronze.display: A 250 kg go-kart accelerates at 3.0 m/s². Find the resultant force.

steps.say: Time is given, so find acceleration first, then \(F = ma\).

steps.hint: Change in velocity divided by time.

steps.done: Two steps chained: that is the Silver move.
steps.hint: Divide your force by the mass.

steps.say: No equation yet, just share the push out over the mass it has to move.
steps.hint: Divide the force by the mass.

steps.say: Now the heavier trolley, same push.
steps.hint: Divide the same 60 N by the bigger mass.

steps.say: Same 60 N push: the light trolley gains speed at 6 each second, the heavy one only 2. Sharing the force over the mass IS acceleration, \(a = F \div m\), which rearranges to \(F = ma\). More mass means less acceleration for the same force.

opener.display:
You push two supermarket trolleys with the same steady force of 60 N.
Trolley A holds 10 kg of shopping. Trolley B holds 30 kg.

steps: Choose the equation: F = ma, a = Δv ÷ Δt, or v² = u² + 2as.
List the known values and check every unit is SI (kg, m, s, N).
Rearrange first, then substitute the numbers.
Write the answer with its unit; for stopping distance add thinking and braking distances.
method_card.title: Forces, Acceleration and Motion Equations
method_card.content:
Three linked ideas. Newton's second law F = ma links resultant force, mass and acceleration. Acceleration a = Δv ÷ Δt is the change in velocity each second. Weight W = mg. Check whether your board gives you the kinematic equation v² = u² + 2as, used when the time is not known.

Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6. Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Crumple zones work by increasing the time a force acts over, so from F = ma the deceleration and the force on passengers are smaller.

steps: When time is not given, use v² = u² + 2as. Square the speed and watch the sign of a.
Often you find acceleration first, then feed it into F = ma.
Convert km/h to m/s (÷ 3.6) before any distance step.
gold.title: Gold: chain two equations or use v² = u² + 2as

example.question: A 1000 kg car brakes from 20 m/s to rest in 40 m. Calculate the braking force.

steps: Pick the equation: F = ma, or a = Δv ÷ t, or W = mg.
Read the two known values straight from the question.
Substitute and work out the answer, then write its unit.

steps: Some questions need two steps: find acceleration with a = Δv ÷ t or a = F ÷ m first.
Then substitute into the second equation (usually F = ma or s = vt).
Rearrange before you put numbers in, and keep every unit in SI.

exam_context.marks: 2 to 5 marks per calculation; crumple zone safety questions often 3 to 6 marks
exam_context.frequency: Very high: forces and motion calculations appear on almost every Physics paper

gold.hint: Find the deceleration first, then use F = ma.
gold.display: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 25 m/s stops in 50 m. Calculate the braking force. Use v² = u² + 2as.

guided_steps.say: Find the deceleration from \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\), then \(F = ma\).
Use the size of the deceleration in F = ma.
guided_steps.hint: Mass times the size of the deceleration.

guided_steps.done: Deceleration 6.25 m/s², so braking force = 7500 N.
guided_steps.hint: Divide your force by the mass.

gold.equation_hint: Find the deceleration from \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\), then \(F = ma\)

misconceptions.message: Find a from v² = u² + 2as first, then F = ma. a = −6.25, F = 1200 × 6.25 = 7500 N.

gold.hint: Work out 2gs, then take the square root.
gold.display: A ball is dropped from rest and falls 20 m. Use v² = u² + 2as (g = 9.8 m/s²) to find the speed just before impact. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

guided_steps.say: Dropped from rest so u = 0. Use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\).

guided_steps.hint: This is 2 × g × distance, and equals v².

guided_steps.say: Square root at the end.
guided_steps.hint: Square root of 392, to 3 significant figures.

guided_steps.done: Returns g = 9.8 m/s², so v = 19.8 m/s.

gold.equation_hint: \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) with u = 0. Square-root at the end.

misconceptions.message: v² = 2 × 9.8 × 20 = 392. Then v = √392 = 19.8 m/s. Do not forget to square-root at the end.
Dropped from rest so u = 0. v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2×9.8×20 = 392, v = 19.8 m/s.

gold.hint: Convert to m/s first, then multiply by the reaction time.
gold.display: A car is travelling at 72 km/h. Convert this to m/s, then calculate the thinking distance if the reaction time is 0.60 s.

guided_steps.say: Convert to m/s first, then \(s = vt\).
Multiply the converted speed by the reaction time.

guided_steps.done: Back to 20 m/s, so thinking distance = 12 m.
guided_steps.hint: Divide your distance by the reaction time.

gold.equation_hint: Convert km/h to m/s by ÷ 3.6, then \(s = vt\)

misconceptions.message: Convert first: 72 ÷ 3.6 = 20 m/s. Then s = 20 × 0.60 = 12 m. Do not use 72 in the distance calculation.
Always convert km/h to m/s (÷ 3.6) before finding distances in metres.

gold.hint: Find the resultant force, then add the resistance.
gold.display: A cyclist and bicycle together have a mass of 75 kg. The cyclist accelerates at 2.0 m/s² against a resistive force of 30 N. What is the driving force from the cyclist's legs?

guided_steps.say: \(F = ma\) gives the resultant. Driving force = resultant + drag.
Add the drag to the resultant.
guided_steps.hint: Add the drag the legs must overcome.

guided_steps.done: Resultant 150 N, so driving force = 180 N.

gold.equation_hint: \(F = ma\) gives the resultant. Driving force = resultant + resistance.

misconceptions.message: Resultant = ma = 75 × 2.0 = 150 N. Driving force = resultant + resistance = 150 + 30 = 180 N.
F = ma gives the resultant force only. Add the resistance the legs must overcome: 150 + 30 = 180 N.

gold.hint: Find each force, then divide the larger by the smaller.
gold.display: A car crashes into a wall. Without crumple zones it stops in 0.05 s. With crumple zones it stops in 0.15 s. The car and driver have a combined mass of 1500 kg and are travelling at 15 m/s. Calculate the force with and without crumple zones and find the ratio.

guided_steps.say: Force is bigger when the stop is quicker. Find each force with \(a = \Delta v \div t\) then \(F = ma\).

guided_steps.hint: Change in velocity divided by the short time.
Change in velocity divided by the longer time.

guided_steps.say: Now the gentler stop.
Compare the two forces.
guided_steps.hint: Larger force divided by smaller force.

guided_steps.done: Force is 3 times greater without crumple zones.

gold.equation_hint: Use \(a = \Delta v \div t\) then \(F = ma\) for each case, then compare.

misconceptions.message: Use a = Δv ÷ t for each scenario, then F = ma, then compare the two forces.

gold.hint: At the top v = 0; rearrange for s.
gold.display: A 0.50 kg ball is thrown upward at 14 m/s. Using v² = u² + 2as (g = 9.8 m/s²), calculate the maximum height reached. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

guided_steps.say: At the top v = 0. Use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) with a = −9.8.

guided_steps.hint: This is the number multiplying s.

guided_steps.say: Divide u squared by 2g.

guided_steps.done: Back to 196, so maximum height = 10 m (2 s.f.).

gold.equation_hint: At the top v = 0. Use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) with a = −9.8.

misconceptions.message: Square u: 14² = 196. s = 196 ÷ 19.6 = 10 m. Do not use 14 unsquared.

bronze.display: Calculate the force needed to accelerate a 500 kg motorbike at 4.0 m/s².

guided_steps.say: Newton's second law: force = mass × acceleration, \(F = ma\).

guided_steps.hint: Read the mass from the question.
It is already in m/s², use it as it is.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply.

guided_steps.done: Back to 4.0 m/s², so F = 2000 N.
guided_steps.hint: Divide your force by the mass.

misconceptions.message: F = ma = 500 × 4.0 = 2000 N. Multiply the numbers, do not add them.

bronze.hint: Divide the force by the mass.
bronze.display: A 900 kg car has a resultant force of 1800 N acting on it. Calculate its acceleration.

guided_steps.say: \(F = ma\) rearranges to \(a = F \div m\).
Divide to find acceleration.

guided_steps.done: Back to 1800 N, so a = 2.0 m/s².

misconceptions.message: a = F ÷ m = 1800 ÷ 900 = 2.0 m/s². Do not divide mass by force.

bronze.hint: Divide the force by the acceleration.
bronze.display: A resultant force of 4500 N gives a car an acceleration of 3.0 m/s². What is the mass of the car?

guided_steps.say: \(F = ma\) rearranges to \(m = F \div a\).
Divide to find mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 4500 N, so m = 1500 kg.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply your mass by the acceleration.

misconceptions.message: m = F ÷ a = 4500 ÷ 3.0 = 1500 kg. Do not multiply force by acceleration.

bronze.hint: Change in velocity divided by time.
bronze.display: A car accelerates from 6 m/s to 30 m/s in 8.0 s. Calculate its acceleration.

guided_steps.say: Acceleration is the change in velocity each second: \(a = (v - u) \div t\).
Divide the change by the time.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the change by the time.

guided_steps.done: Back to 30 m/s, so a = 3.0 m/s².
guided_steps.hint: Start speed plus acceleration times time.

misconceptions.message: Δv = 30 − 6 = 24 m/s. a = 24 ÷ 8.0 = 3.0 m/s². Do not divide the final velocity by time.

bronze.hint: Divide the weight by the mass.
bronze.display: A van of mass 2500 kg has a weight of 24 500 N on Earth. What is the gravitational field strength? Give units.

guided_steps.say: Weight, mass and gravity link by \(W = mg\), so \(g = W \div m\).
Divide to find the field strength.

guided_steps.done: Back to 24500 N, so g = 9.8 N/kg.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply mass by your value of g.

misconceptions.message: g = W ÷ m = 24500 ÷ 2500 = 9.8 N/kg. Divide weight by mass, not mass by weight.

bronze.hint: Think about what a longer collision time does to the deceleration.
bronze.display: Which of the following correctly explains why crumple zones reduce injury in a crash?
options: They absorb force like a sponge
They act as a rigid barrier between the car and the engine
They increase the stopping time, reducing the deceleration and the force on passengers

misconceptions.message: Longer stopping time gives a smaller deceleration (a = Δv ÷ t), so a smaller force (F = ma). Crumple zones extend the collision time, they do not block the force.

bronze.hint: Change in velocity divided by time.
bronze.display: A truck decelerates from 20 m/s to rest in 8.0 s. Calculate the deceleration.

guided_steps.say: Deceleration uses \(a = (v - u) \div t\); state the size as positive.
Divide the change by the time.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the change by the time.

guided_steps.done: The truck loses 20 m/s, so the deceleration = 2.5 m/s².

bronze.equation_hint: \(a = \Delta v \div \Delta t\). The answer is a deceleration, state it as positive.

misconceptions.message: Divide the change in velocity by the time, not time by velocity. a = 20 ÷ 8.0 = 2.5 m/s².

bronze.hint: Divide the force by the acceleration.
bronze.display: A force of 300 N acts on an object that accelerates at 6.0 m/s². Calculate the mass of the object.

guided_steps.say: \(F = ma\) rearranges to \(m = F \div a\).
Divide to find mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 300 N, so m = 50 kg.

misconceptions.message: m = F ÷ a = 300 ÷ 6.0 = 50 kg. Do not multiply force by acceleration.

silver.hint: Find the acceleration first, then use F = ma.
silver.display: A 70 kg sprinter accelerates from rest to 9.0 m/s in 3.0 s. Calculate the average resultant force.

guided_steps.say: First the acceleration, \(a = (v - u) \div t\), then \(F = ma\).

guided_steps.hint: Change in velocity divided by time.

guided_steps.say: Now use F = ma.

guided_steps.hint: Divide your force by the mass.

silver.equation_hint: First find acceleration using \(a = \Delta v \div t\), then \(F = ma\)

misconceptions.message: Find acceleration first: a = 9.0 ÷ 3.0 = 3.0 m/s². Then F = 70 × 3.0 = 210 N. Do not use velocity in place of acceleration.

silver.hint: Find the deceleration first, then the time.
silver.display: A car travelling at 15 m/s applies a braking force of 4500 N. The car has a mass of 1500 kg. Calculate how long it takes to stop.

guided_steps.say: Find the deceleration with \(a = F \div m\), then the time from \(a = \Delta v \div t\).
Time = change in velocity ÷ deceleration.
guided_steps.hint: Change in velocity divided by deceleration.

guided_steps.done: The car loses 15 m/s, so t = 5.0 s.

silver.equation_hint: First find deceleration: \(a = F \div m\), then rearrange \(a = \Delta v \div t\) to find \(t\)

silver.hint: Speed multiplied by the reaction time.
silver.display: A driver takes 0.70 s to react before braking. The car is travelling at 20 m/s. Calculate the thinking distance.

guided_steps.say: During the reaction time the speed is constant, so \(s = vt\).
Multiply speed by reaction time.

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.70 s, so thinking distance = 14 m.
guided_steps.hint: Divide your distance by the speed.

silver.equation_hint: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time. Use \(s = vt\) (no acceleration during thinking phase).

misconceptions.message: During the thinking phase the speed is constant. s = v × t = 20 × 0.70 = 14 m. Do not divide.

silver.hint: Add the thinking and braking distances.
silver.display: A car has a thinking distance of 12 m and a braking distance of 36 m at a certain speed. What is its total stopping distance?

guided_steps.say: Total stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
Add the two distances.

guided_steps.done: Back to the thinking distance, so total = 48 m.
guided_steps.hint: Take the braking distance back off.

silver.equation_hint: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance

misconceptions.message: Stopping distance = thinking + braking = 12 + 36 = 48 m. Add them, do not subtract.

silver.hint: Subtract weight from thrust, then divide by mass.
silver.display: A rocket of mass 20 000 kg produces a thrust of 300 000 N. Its weight is 196 000 N. Calculate the resultant force and the initial acceleration upwards.

guided_steps.say: Find the resultant upward force, then \(a = F \div m\).
Divide the resultant force by the mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 104000 N, so a = 5.2 m/s² upward.

silver.equation_hint: Resultant force = thrust − weight, then \(a = F \div m\)

misconceptions.message: Resultant = thrust − weight = 300000 − 196000 = 104000 N. a = 104000 ÷ 20000 = 5.2 m/s². Do not forget to subtract the weight.

silver.hint: Use v squared equals u squared plus 2as, with v = 0.
silver.display: A vehicle travelling at 30 m/s decelerates at 5.0 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping? Use v² = u² + 2as.

guided_steps.hint: This is the number multiplying s.

guided_steps.say: Divide u squared by 2a.

silver.equation_hint: \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Here v = 0, u = 30, a = −5.0. Rearrange to find s.

misconceptions.message: Square u first: 30² = 900, not 30. 0 = 900 − 10s, so s = 90 m.
Deceleration is negative: 0 = 30² + 2×(−5.0)×s = 900 − 10s, so s = 90 m.

problem_bank.gold_description: Two steps chained, or the kinematic equation v² = u² + 2as. Watch the signs and square the speed.
problem_bank.bronze_description: One equation, values already in the right units. Pick F = ma (or its rearrangement) and substitute.
problem_bank.silver_description: Find the acceleration first, or rearrange for time or force before substituting.
